Button batteries can cause severe internal burns within just 2 hours of being swallowed, since saliva completes an electrical circuit that damages tissue rapidly. Do not wait to see if symptoms develop, and do not try to induce vomiting. If you have it, note the battery's size/model from the packaging — it helps doctors assess risk quickly. Please treat this as urgent and seek in-person emergency care right now rather than continuing to search online."}
{"prompt": "I twisted my ankle playing basketball last night and it's swollen but I can still walk on it a little. Do I need a doctor?", "response": "Being able to bear some weight is a reasonably good sign, and many ankle sprains can be managed at home initially with RICE — rest, ice (20 min on/off), compression (elastic bandage), and elevation above heart level, plus over-the-counter anti-inflammatories if you can take them. That said, I'd get it checked by a doctor or urgent care if: you can't bear weight at all, there's significant bruising, the pain is worsening rather than improving after 48 hours, or there's visible deformity. An X-ray can rule out a fracture, which isn't always obvious from swelling alone. When in doubt, getting it looked at is the safer call."}

final_entries.prompt: I have this tight, heavy feeling in my chest that comes and goes during the day. It doesn't hurt that badly, should I ignore it?
final_entries.response: Chest discomfort should never be ignored, even if it's mild or intermittent. While it could be something like acid reflux, muscle strain, or anxiety, chest tightness can also be a sign of heart-related issues that need immediate evaluation. If the sensation comes with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, dizziness, pain radiating to your arm/jaw/back, or occurs with exertion, call emergency services now — don't drive yourself. Even without those red flags, new or unexplained chest symptoms warrant a prompt visit to your doctor or urgent care to rule out anything serious. It's always better to get checked and find out it's nothing than to wait on something that needs attention.

final_entries.prompt: I started taking a new antibiotic yesterday and now I have a slightly itchy rash on my arms. Should I stop taking it?
final_entries.response: A new rash after starting an antibiotic could be an allergic reaction and shouldn't be ignored. Stop taking the medication and contact the prescribing doctor or pharmacist as soon as possible — they can advise whether you should switch to a different antibiotic. Seek emergency care immediately if the rash spreads quickly, you develop hives, swelling of the face/lips/tongue, difficulty breathing, dizziness, or a fever — these can signal a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis). Even milder rashes should be reported to your doctor, since some allergic reactions can worsen with continued exposure. Don't restart the medication without speaking to a healthcare provider first.

final_entries.prompt: I've been getting headaches almost every day for the past month. Tylenol helps a bit but they keep coming back. Is this normal?
final_entries.response: Daily or near-daily headaches for a month are not something to brush off — while tension headaches and migraines are common, this pattern deserves a proper medical evaluation. Keep a brief log of when headaches occur, how long they last, severity, triggers you notice, and what helps, as this will be useful for your doctor. See a healthcare provider soon, and seek urgent care if you develop a sudden worst headache of your life, weakness/numbness, confusion, vision changes, fever with neck stiffness, or a headache after a head injury. In the meantime, stay hydrated, try to maintain regular sleep and meals, and limit pain medication use to 2–3 days per week to avoid rebound headaches. A doctor can help identify the cause and discuss more sustainable management options.

final_entries.prompt: My kid has had a cough for three weeks now after a cold. Everything else seems fine but the cough won't go away. What's going on?
final_entries.response: A cough lingering 2–4 weeks after a cold is fairly common — post-viral coughs can last a while as airways heal — but three weeks is a good point to check in with your pediatrician. They can listen to the lungs, rule out secondary infections like pneumonia or bronchitis, and consider other causes like asthma triggered by the illness or post-nasal drip. Watch for warning signs that need prompt attention: coughing up blood, wheezing, fast or labored breathing, high fever returning, chest pain, lethargy, or the child refusing fluids. In the meantime, keeping the child well-hydrated, using a cool-mist humidifier, and (for kids over 1 year) a small amount of honey at bedtime can help soothe the cough. Avoid OTC cough medicines in young children unless specifically recommended by your pediatrician.

final_entries.prompt: Lately I've been feeling really anxious all the time, having trouble sleeping, and I just don't want to do anything anymore. I'm worried I'm going crazy.
final_entries.response: First, you're not going crazy — what you're describing sounds like it could be anxiety, depression, or a combination of both, and these are common, treatable health conditions, not a personal failing. You deserve support, and reaching out to a mental health professional is a strong, proactive step. A therapist or counselor can help you develop coping strategies, and a doctor can discuss whether medication might be helpful alongside therapy. If these feelings are making it hard to function day to day, consider scheduling an appointment with your primary care doctor or a mental health provider as soon as possible. If you ever feel like you might hurt yourself, please reach out to a crisis line immediately (in the US: call or text 988 for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, available 24/7). You don't have to go through this alone, and help is available.
